# gptr <picture><source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Broccolito/gptr/main/man/figures/logo-dark.png"/><img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Broccolito/gptr/main/man/figures/logo.png" align="right" width="120" height="139" alt="gptr logo"/></picture>

gptr runs language model agents inside your live R session, through one function: `peter()`.
With a prompt it returns an R object; with no prompt it opens a chat in the console.

## Your live R session

The agent's R code runs in your R process, in the environment `peter()` is called from (at the
console, your workspace). It works on the objects already in memory, so you do not save data to
a file for it or rerun a script to rebuild state. What the agent creates, such as a fitted
model, is an ordinary R object that you and the next prompt can use. The model gets a bounded
view (`?gptr_egress`): your prompt, a workspace listing, a short description of each object you
pass (class, dimensions, column types, a few values) and the output of the code it runs. R
computes on the full object. In a measured run, three read-only tool calls on a 4 GiB vector
kept R's memory peak at 4.2 GiB; code that modifies an object follows R's usual copy-on-modify
rules.

## System 1 and System 2

gptr works with two kinds of model. System 2 models are conversational: they run the agent
loop, call tools and return a session that `|>` continues. System 1 models are typed decision
models: they return an R vector with one answer per input (logical for a yes/no question,
character for `choices`, numeric for `levels`) with the probabilities attached. `peter()` picks
System 1 or System 2 from the model you pass. System 2 runs on Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini,
OpenRouter and other OpenAI-compatible APIs, Azure, Bedrock, the Claude Code and Codex CLIs,
and local Ollama models. System 1 runs on TypeSafe AI's Jev, or on Clef and Clef Flash through
a local Ollama server.

## Sessions as runnable documents

A model-assisted analysis should be as reproducible as one written by hand, so gptr records the
procedure as it actually ran. Bind an R script, R Markdown, Quarto or Jupyter file with
`gptr_doc()`, and gptr writes the R code the agent ran below each prompt, under a header with
the model, date, tokens and hashes of the prompt and code. The file is the record, and it runs.
Rerun it without a model or API key, ask again with your own model (`replay = "live"`), or turn
a recorded `.R` file into an ordinary R script with `gptr_export()`. Records are plain files you
own; there is no gptr server, account or central store. Commit one with your code or publish it
with a paper: anyone can rerun it to reproduce the analysis, or re-ask it with their own model
to replicate it. The record is the basis gptr provides for reproducible scientific computing
and research.

## Installation

Install gptr from CRAN, or the development version from GitHub. It is pure R, with no compiled
code, and needs R 4.2 or later.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("gptr")
pak::pak("Broccolito/gptr")
```

This README describes gptr 1.0.0; if `packageVersion("gptr")` is lower, install from GitHub.
If pak stops with `Subprocess is busy or cannot start`, or a later call reports a missing or
corrupt `gptr.rdb`, restart R and install again before loading gptr, or use
`remotes::install_github("Broccolito/gptr")`.

## Connect a model

Sign in to the Claude Code or Codex CLI outside R, then call `peter()` at the console to open a
chat. With no model set, it offers those routes and saves your choice. For an API provider, load
its key from a `.env` file and pick a model:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gptr_env("~/keys/.env")
gptr_config(model = "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5", .scope = "user")
```

`gptr_env()` loads keys such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY` and, for
Jev, `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`; `gptr_providers()` lists what is configured. The first time you use a
remote provider at the console, gptr shows what it sends and asks you to acknowledge it.

With Ollama running and the model pulled, `model = "ollama/qwen3:1.7b"` or another installed
model with tool calls runs the agent, and `model = "ollama/clef-flash"` (Ollama 0.35.1 or later)
answers typed decisions. gptr never installs Ollama, pulls models or falls back to a cloud model.

## A first session

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(gptr)
gptr_doc("analysis.R")
session = peter("Fit mpg on wt in mtcars and store the model as fit.")
session |> peter("Which cars have the largest residuals in fit?")
gptr_doc(FALSE)
```

The second prompt reuses `fit`, which is now in your workspace, and `analysis.R` holds both
prompts and the code that ran. In a new R session, `gptr_source("analysis.R", replay = "replay")`
rebuilds `fit` from that file without calling a model. In the default `manual` mode, read-only
code runs directly and changes to objects or files ask first; the check is advisory, not a
sandbox (`?gptr_security`).

A System 1 model answers with a typed vector:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
abstracts = c("We randomized 200 adults to drug or placebo.",
              "We followed 5000 nurses for 20 years.")
is_rct = peter("Is this a randomized trial?", abstracts, model = "jev")
gptr_prob(is_rct)
```

`is_rct` is a logical vector, one answer per abstract, so `abstracts[is_rct]` keeps the trials.

## Learn more

Start with `vignette("getting-started", package = "gptr")`; its examples run offline with
`gptr_fake_provider()`. The longer examples are in the guides:

- [Execution model](https://broccolito.github.io/gptr/articles/execution-model.html): what the
  model receives, memory and large objects.
- [Language models](https://broccolito.github.io/gptr/articles/language-models.html): providers,
  keys, CLIs and Ollama.
- [System 1 decisions](https://broccolito.github.io/gptr/articles/system-one.html): choices,
  scores, thresholds and probabilities, with an offline demo.
- [Script as history](https://broccolito.github.io/gptr/articles/script-as-history.html):
  recording, replay and export.
- [Interactive console](https://broccolito.github.io/gptr/articles/interactive-console.html):
  the chat, steering and slash commands.

Every guide, the function reference and a
[cheat sheet](https://broccolito.github.io/gptr/cheatsheet.html) are on the
[package site](https://broccolito.github.io/gptr/).

## Why Peter?

`peter()` is named for two Peters. Peter Cathcart Wason studied dual processes in reasoning
with Jonathan Evans; gptr's System 1 and System 2 refer to that line of work. The labels are
software roles: they imply nothing about human cognition, and Wason did not introduce them.
Peter Naur edited the ALGOL 60 report, whose notation is now called Backus-Naur Form; in that
spirit, gptr records sessions as documents you can read and run. The
[Why Peter?](https://broccolito.github.io/gptr/articles/why-peter.html) guide gives the history
and sources.

## Upgrading from gptr 0.7.0

gptr 1.0.0 is a rewrite. `get_response()` and `dataframe_to_text()` are gone: use
`peter("your prompt")$text`, and pass a data frame to `peter()` as context. See `NEWS.md`.

## License and acknowledgments

gptr is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. Third-party notices are in `inst/COPYRIGHTS`.

gptr was inspired by Mario Zechner's 'pi' coding agent. The tool descriptions, edit guidelines
and prompt-template grammar are derived from 'pi', the model catalog from models.dev and the
secret patterns from gitleaks, and the System 1 emulation prompt follows TypeSafe AI's
system-one-adapter-python. All four are MIT-licensed. Ideas came from 'ellmer', 'tidyllm',
'btw' and 'mcptools', none of which gptr depends on. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, TypeSafe AI,
Ollama and the vendors of the command-line tools are third-party services; gptr is not
affiliated with or endorsed by them.
